draft.title: Language modes
card: Page
A reader can see the whole text, slow down and reread. Writers can use longer sentences, paragraphs, headings and layout.
Speaking aloud
A listener hears each word once and cannot go back. Speakers use shorter sentences, repetition, rhythm and direct address such as "you" to keep listeners following.
Screen
Screen readers often scan. Writers may use short chunks, headings, links, images or sound to carry meaning.
Why it matters
The same idea is shaped differently in each mode, because the way the audience takes it in is different.
draft.remember: Shape a piece for how its audience will take it in: reading, listening or scanning.

a.q: Why would a speechwriter repeat a main phrase several times in a speech?
opts: Listeners hear it once and need it to stick
Readers can scan the repeated phrase easily
Repetition lets the speaker use longer sentences
A speech needs the layout of a printed page
a.why: Listeners cannot go back, so repetition helps them follow and remember. The option about scanning describes readers on a screen, not an audience listening to a speech.
a.clue: Think about what a listener cannot do.

b.q: Priya turns her essay for a printed magazine into a school podcast script. Which change best suits the new mode?
opts: Shorten the sentences and speak directly to listeners
Keep the long sentences so nothing is lost
Add subheadings so listeners can see the layout
Add links so listeners can click to read more
b.why: Listeners hear the words once, so short sentences and direct address help them follow. Headings and links work for readers who can see a page or screen, not for listeners of a podcast.
b.clue: A listener cannot see layout or click.

a.best: Listeners hear it once and need it to stick

b.best: Shorten the sentences and speak directly to listeners

problems.detail: "Screen readers often scan" is ambiguous, because "screen reader" is also the name of assistive software that reads text aloud for vision-impaired users. "People reading on a screen often scan" would avoid the confusion.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer, and the explanations match the card. The only problem is the phrase "Screen readers" on the card, which could be mistaken for assistive reading software.
